claim: Superforecasters selected on one year of GJP scores stayed far more accurate than other forecasters in later years, with no regression to the mean (standardized Brier -0.34 vs -0.14 top-team individuals vs +0.04 all others, Years 2-3 average; AUC 96 vs 75). Confounded with elite-team support and heavier workload. All from one research group.
agent_test: Pick the best-scoring prompt/scaffold variant on question set 1, re-run on fresh set 2 at equal tokens; check whether its edge shrinks.

claim: About 70% of superforecasters kept status next year and year-to-year accuracy correlation is .65. Both figures come only from the popular book (Superforecasting p.104) via the AI Impacts blog; neither appears in the Mellers 2015 paper text (re-checked). Treat as second-hand. Gap search: the Mellers 2017 JDM paper (opened) has no year-to-year r or retention percentage either; primary source still not found.
agent_test: Do not use as a target. Measure our own test-retest r of agent Brier across two disjoint question sets.

claim: In the IARPA Hybrid Forecasting Competition Season 1 (326 forecasters), the same accuracy metric across two halves of 188 questions (94 each) correlated .36 (simple), .41 (hierarchical) and .36 (IRT), which the authors took as moderate evidence that accuracy is stable over time; a small independent tournament (195 fully engaged of 314 registered, 14 questions) confirmed 2 people at the top 2% and 38 at the top 25%, so persistence is supported but thinly.
agent_test: Split-half r of an agent variant's Brier across question halves; size the question set so r is at least .6 before comparing variants.
audit_note: Numbers match (Himmelstein Table 2 same-metric across halves .36 / .41 / .36; small tournament 314 registered, 195 engaged, 2 confirmed at top 2%, 38 at 25%), but the authors read these correlations as supporting temporal stability of accuracy, and the '.65 headline' comparison is not in the Himmelstein paper, so 'well below' and 'noisy guide' are the notes' own interpretation.
claim_before_audit: In an independent replication (IARPA HFC, 326 forecasters), the same accuracy metric across two halves of 94 questions correlated only about .36 to .41, well below the .65 headline. Persistence exists but one season is a noisy guide to skill. Gap search: a small independent tournament (n=195, 14 questions) confirmed only 2 people at top 2% and 38 at top 25%, with no luck null test, so persistence is supported but thin.

claim: Past performance becomes the best predictor of future forecast accuracy after about 20 resolved questions and keeps adding up to 80+; IRT/hierarchical models explain R2 about .48-.57 in Season 1 (only .35 at 80 questions in Season 2).
agent_test: Give the agent a running per-domain Brier record and test if conditioning on it (shrink toward base rate when record is poor) beats no record.

claim: Trait predictors of accuracy (fluid intelligence, numeracy, CRT, open-mindedness, political knowledge) are real but small (r about .1-.3 in GJP and HFC). Open-mindedness and education did not replicate from HFC Season 1 to Season 2 (AOMT r .13-.17 to .00-.04, partly low reliability).
schema_part: none (human traits; no direct agent mapping)
agent_test: Closest analogue: does a stronger base model give better Brier at equal tokens (see K14).
audit_note: Mellers 2015 GJP correlations are .07 to .23 and HFC Season 1 .11 to .22; Season 2 AOMT .00-.04 and education -.03 to -.08 confirmed; Chang 2016 was not opened.

claim: Brief probability training (under 1 hour; CHAMPS KNOW) improved Brier 6-12% over control in each of four randomized tournament years, shrinking from 10-12% (Y1-2) to 6-7% (Y3-4). Same group; no outside RCT replication found. Not re-opened by the cross-checker. Gap search: an IRT re-analysis (Hauenstein et al., Psychological Science, abstract only) says the Y1-2 training and teaming effects shrink or reverse once extraneous method variables are controlled; a 20-minute extra training arm gave no significant extra top forecasters (n=86 vs 109).
agent_test: Compare an agent with a comparison-class-and-update checklist against none at equal tokens. See K16: prompt analogues showed no gain.

claim: Of the ten CHAMPS KNOW principles, only comparison classes (outside view / base rates) were reliably linked to better forecasts; post-mortem and some others were linked to worse scores (likely reverse causation). Self-reported, correlational.
agent_test: Ablate a base-rate-first step alone vs the full checklist at equal tokens on resolved binary questions.

claim: Teaming (shared news and rationales) beat crowd-belief polling, which beat independent forecasting, with large effects (Y1 F(2,1586)=60.68); comment counts correlated r=-.19 to -.22 with Brier. Groupthink not found, not ruled out. Gap search: the same IRT re-analysis challenges the teaming effect too (abstract only; effect sizes not read).
agent_test: Compare N independent samples averaged vs N samples that see each other's rationales and revise, at equal tokens.

claim: Superforecasters use finer probability steps (57 unique values vs 29-30), and rounding to the nearest 0.10 hurt their Brier but not the other groups' (granularity may be a marker, not a cause).
agent_test: Round agent probabilities to 0.1 vs 0.01 and compare Brier at equal tokens.

claim: Forecasters in the geopolitical tournament were overconfident, worst on 100% forecasts made early in a question's life (about 70% right early vs about 90% late, Mellers 2014, figure not rechecked); extremizing the aggregate improved Brier (high-expertise mean a=2.43, .187 to .148; Baron et al.) and is supported by partial-information theory (Satopaa et al.); post-hoc Platt recalibration helped live bots (Brier gain .016 binary); for LLM ensembles a fixed Platt coefficient of about 1.73 gave Brier .1119 to .1076 on FB-7-21 (AIA), the best factor differs (1.72 for superforecasters, 2.27 for AIA), and Murphy found no statistically resolved overall gain from Platt scaling for its main backbone.
agent_test: Apply extremizing and Platt recalibration to an agent ensemble on held-out questions at equal tokens.
audit_note: Verified: Baron et al. (mean a=2.43, Brier .148 vs .187 for high-expertise forecasters), AIA (fixed 1.73, .1119 to .1076; 1.72 supers, 2.27 AIA), LessWrong (Platt gain .016 binary); not verified: Mellers 70%/90% figure and the 'mainly because' causal wording (full text blocked); Murphy reports no statistically resolved Platt gain for the main backbone overall, with small gains (+0.72/+1.48 BI) on a preliminary model, not specifically 'when a crowd price is in context'.
claim_before_audit: Forecasters were overconfident mainly because early extreme (100%) forecasts were not updated (right about 70% early, about 90% late); extremizing the aggregate improves Brier (mean a=2.43, .187 to .148) and is supported by partial-information theory. Post-hoc Platt recalibration helped live bots (Brier gain .016 binary). Gap search: for LLM ensembles a fixed Platt/extremizing coefficient of about 1.73 gave Brier .1119 to .1076 on FB-7-21 (AIA), but the factor that is best differs (1.72 supers, 2.27 AIA) and a second system (Murphy) found no resolved gain when a crowd price is in context.

claim: Plain frontier LLMs without retrieval were near or worse than coin flip on post-cutoff questions (best zero-shot GPT-4-1106 .208 vs crowd .149 vs random .25); a retrieval plus ensemble pipeline reached .179, still behind the crowd, and beat it only when the crowd was unsure (.199 vs .246 on validation). Re-verified in the PDF.
agent_test: Equal-token ablation: no retrieval vs retrieval vs retrieval+ensemble; report Brier by crowd-uncertainty bin.

claim: Halawi ablation: removing fine-tuning gave .186 and removing both fine-tuning and retrieval gave .206 (baseline .208), so retrieval carried most of the gain. Differences of .003-.007 are near standard errors; table row labels in the PDF text are partly garbled.
agent_test: As K11 ablation.

claim: A median of 12 LLMs matched a 925-person human crowd on 31 Metaculus questions (Brier .20 vs .19, p=.85, wide equivalence bounds), with a yes/acquiescence bias (median forecast 60%, about 45% resolved yes). Showing LLMs the human median improved them 17-28%, but plain averaging with humans was better. Gap search: same-model samples are highly correlated, and across-model mixing beat repeating the best model at a fixed sample count (N=113); averaging 10 samples of one system beat one sample (.1140 vs .1182). Neither is an equal-token test against one long chain.
agent_test: Median of differently prompted/different-model samples vs best single, at equal total tokens; check acquiescence bias against base rate.

claim: On leakage-free ForecastBench, superforecasters (.096, 39 people) beat the public (.121) and the best LLM Claude 3.5 Sonnet (.122); gap shrinking about .015-.017 Brier per year, projected parity late 2026 to mid 2027 with wide intervals (linear extrapolation, few models).
agent_test: Run our agent on ForecastBench dataset questions as an external score.
audit_note: The ForecastBench paper and the 'closing the gap' post are both from the Forecasting Research Institute, so the trend and parity projection rest on one organisation; also the source gives the gap (0.017) and the LLM improvement (0.015 in a year), a point estimate of Nov 2026 with 95% CI Jan 2026 to Nov 2027, not 'late 2026 to mid 2027'. Brier numbers (.096, .121, .122, 39 supers) verified.

claim: Metaculus bot-vs-Pro tournaments: Pros led best bots every quarter (-11.3, -8.9, -17.7, -20.0 peer points), no sign of closing; scaffolded bots beat the plain template of the same model by 5-11 points; winners used more research sources (r=.42) and aggregation, about 28 LLM calls vs 7 (survey, correlational).
agent_test: Replicate on the Metaculus AI benchmark: plain vs scaffolded with equal calls.

claim: Prompt tricks do not help LLM forecasting: of 38 prompts (persona, base rate first, premortem, CoT) none beat noise after correction; Bayesian-reasoning prompts made Brier worse (+.03) by pushing forecasts away from 0.5. Pratt 2024 also found personas and news worse than baseline. Corrected after reading the paper: none beat control in the preregistered mixed model except two harmful prompts; in paired t-tests three base-rate-style prompts (Frequency-Based, Base Rate First -0.016, Step-Back) survive correction with small gains. Harm from the Bayesian prompt is not explained by distance from 0.5 alone (Chain of Thought was as decisive, 17-20 points, and not significantly harmful).
schema_part: O (do not add persona/Bayes prompts); section 4b
agent_test: Test our base-rate and Bayes operators against a plain prompt at equal tokens with multiple-comparison correction.
audit_note: Numbers match Schoenegger et al. (Bayesian Reasoning +0.03, Propose-Evaluate-Select +0.033, Base Rate First -0.016 paired after BH) and Pratt (multiple personas and news API worse than baseline); the claim's 'none beat noise' headline is qualified correctly in its own correction text.

claim: An LLM assistant raised human accuracy 24-28% in a preregistered study (N=991) even when noisy and overconfident; the control was a weaker model and one outlier item drove part of the effect.
agent_test: Not an agent-scaffold test.

claim: Outcome-trained models improve forecasting: Brier-reward RL gave a 14B model .190 (matches o1) and DPO on resolved outcomes gave +7-10% accuracy, but market price stayed better by about .04. This is training, not scaffold.
agent_test: Out of scope; only a calibration layer (Platt) is scaffold-compatible.

claim: LLM forecasting claims are fragile: at least 3.8% of Halawi's questions resolved early, at least 10% of Tao et al. were trivial given the cut date; date-limited search leaks. Brier is not comparable across question sets.
agent_test: Use only questions opened after model cutoff; log retrieval dates; report Brier relative to a base-rate forecaster.

claim: The Lu 2025 expert advantage (Brier .0225 vs o3 .1352) compares a median of per-question expert Brier scores with a mean model Brier. The experts' own mean Brier is .1573 (157 q) and .1222 (41 q), on different subsets than the models' 464-q mean. The advantage is not established by that paper's numbers. Gap search: no redo of the Lu comparison found. On identical ForecastBench questions with mean Brier, a scaffolded system (AIA) matched the superforecaster median (.1076 vs .1110).
agent_test: Rerun models and experts on identical questions with the same statistic (mean Brier, paired test).

claim: Logical consistency (negation, paraphrase, conditional checks) correlates with later Brier (r .49-.92 depending on metric), but training for consistency did not improve accuracy; part of the correlation is that stronger models are both.
agent_test: Add a negation/complement consistency check and test whether using it as filter or average improves Brier at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Short adaptive cognitive-test batteries predicted forecast error at r about -.67 to -.71 in lay samples on time-series questions, much higher than HFC trait correlations (.1-.3), probably because tests and tasks are matched.
agent_test: Not agent-testable.

claim: Question difficulty explains 62.2% of the variance in per-question LLM forecast scores and method only 2.7% (12 agent methods, 400 questions, 5 trials). Scaffold comparisons therefore need paired designs. By my calculation, detecting a 0.01 Brier gap needs about 650 to 1,500 questions at a paired SD of 0.10-0.15 per question, about 200-450 for a 0.02 gap (fewer with 5-10 samples per question).
agent_test: Measure per-question paired SD of our own scaffold vs plain, then size the question set from it. Report test-retest r of the Brier difference across two disjoint question sets.

claim: Averaging several independent runs of one forecasting system beats a single run (Brier .1182 single vs .1140 mean of 10; diminishing returns after about 5), while probabilities from different frontier models are highly correlated, so mixing models or pipelines gives more than repeating the best one. No test holds total tokens equal against one long chain of thought.
agent_test: At equal total tokens compare: 1 long chain, 5 short samples of one prompt, 5 short samples with different prompts or retrieval paths.
audit_note: Aitchison et al. find the value of mixing comes from less-correlated models (Grok 4, fine-tuned model) rather than frontier models in general; 'no token-matched test' is an absence claim not checkable.

claim: Reconciling disagreement among forecasts with a supervisor that searches for new evidence beat picking the best forecast and beat the mean in one system (.1125 vs .1199), but another system found LLM-judge aggregation worse than a simple mean. Effect is benchmark-dependent.
agent_test: Compare plain mean against a disagreement-triggered evidence search on the same questions, with and without a crowd price in context.

claim: Post-hoc Platt scaling (log-odds extremizing) helps LLM ensembles when no external crowd anchor is present: Brier .1119 to .1076 with a fixed coefficient of about 1.73, to .1071 fitted leave-one-out, but only .1104 when fitted on another benchmark. Best coefficient differed between superforecasters (1.72) and the LLM system (2.27). With a market price in context another system found no resolved gain.
agent_test: Hold out questions, compare no correction, fixed 1.73, and fitted factor; repeat on a second question source.

claim: A small independent GJP-style tournament (195 engaged forecasters, 14 questions) confirmed 2 people at top 2% and 38 at top 25% across an identification and confirmation phase, with no luck-null test. An extra 20 minutes of training gave no significant increase in top forecasters.
agent_test: None; use as a reminder that top-2% claims at small N are fragile.

claim: In lab tasks outside forecasting, superforecasters tied or beat others on consistency, discrimination and coherence; correlations among these measures averaged .20 (range .08-.39) and the composite related to super status at .46 and .60 (.73 and .82 corrected for unreliability). Supports a moderately unified trait, not a single factor.
agent_test: Check whether an agent's paraphrase and negation consistency on forecasting questions predicts its later Brier (links to K21).

claim: Pre-GJP baseline (second-hand from Wikipedia, book not opened): 284 experts, about 28,000 forecasts 1984-2003; experts slightly better than chance, usually worse than simple extrapolation at 3-5 years; foxes beat hedgehogs; media-famous experts were least accurate.
agent_test: None.

claim: Whether giving an LLM agent its own running per-domain Brier history helps is untested in the sources found. A compact summarised belief state matched a full history within a question (CI includes zero), and one agent system reports gains from distilling outcomes into skills (abstract only, leaderboard rating, not Brier).
agent_test: Run the same question stream with and without a per-domain calibration table in context; paired Brier on the later half.
